steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a fast, event-by-event optical flow method for event cameras that is inspired by neuroscience models of motion detection. Contrast it with packet-based and existing event-by-event approaches and state our contributions.

- Our approach: triplet matching from neuroscience, and contributions
- Link back to neuroscience models

  - reasons: tailored hardware, strong scene assumptions, limited problem settings, hard to define event-by-event benchmarks on real data at microsecond resolution
  - need event-by-event algorithms for complex real-world problems

  - vs batch-based: only three events (triplet) -> future real-time incremental motion estimation
  - vs event-by-event: tested on public optical flow benchmarks, real-world scenes, comparable results
  - logical operations -> simple, efficient data structure; runs on standard CPUs
  - contributions: (i) novel event-by-event algorithm derived from neuroscience; (ii) comparable to prior work, CPU only, faster than optimization-based methods (Fig. 1)

  - signal processing here materializes ideas of current neuroscience models
  - sheds light on strong and weak scenarios -> improve the models

steps.text:
Event cameras have made people rethink visual processing for many computer vision tasks, because the way they operate and the data they output are fundamentally different from conventional frame-based cameras. These sensors are bio-inspired and they naturally respond to the dynamics of the scene. They have advantages like low latency, high dynamic range (HDR) and data efficiency, but new algorithms are needed to unlock these advantages. Neuromorphic principles have been a big source of inspiration for such new algorithms and hardware, especially for motion estimation tasks.

Event-based optical flow estimation methods can be roughly split into packet-based and event-by-event–based methods, depending on how the events are processed and how they update the output of the estimator. Packet-based methods process a batch of events, for example the events in a fixed time window (say 10–100 ms) or a fixed number of events (typically 30k–1M), so they need to wait some time before the processing (inference) can start. So they trade off the high-speed advantages of event data for accuracy. Prior work has proposed adaptations of classical frame-based methods (block matching, Lucas-Kanade), spatio-temporal plane-fitting, time-surface matching, and contrast-maximization methods. They are inspired by frame-based ANN architectures, so they need the data to be converted into a tensor representation, like voxel grids. ANNs achieve the current state-of-the-art accuracy for optical flow estimation and also high speed, but they need power-hungry GPUs and they lack interpretability.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Event cameras have made people rethink visual processing for many computer vision tasks, because the way they operate and the data they output are fundamentally different from conventional frame-based cameras. These sensors are bio-inspired and they naturally respond to the dynamics of the scene. They have advantages like low latency, high dynamic range (HDR) and data efficiency, but new algorithms are needed to unlock these advantages. Neuromorphic principles have been a big source of inspiration for such new algorithms and hardware, especially for motion estimation tasks.

Event-based optical flow estimation methods can be roughly split into packet-based and event-by-event–based methods, depending on how the events are processed and how they update the output of the estimator. Packet-based methods process a batch of events, for example the events in a fixed time window (say 10–100 ms) or a fixed number of events (typically 30k–1M), so they need to wait some time before the processing (inference) can start. So they trade off the high-speed advantages of event data for accuracy. Prior work has proposed adaptations of classical frame-based methods (block matching, Lucas-Kanade), spatio-temporal plane-fitting, time-surface matching, and contrast-maximization methods. These are all model-based (optimization) methods. Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) are batch-based too. They are inspired by frame-based ANN architectures, so they need the data to be converted into a tensor representation, like voxel grids. ANNs achieve the current state-of-the-art accuracy for optical flow estimation and also high speed, but they need power-hungry GPUs and they lack interpretability.

Event-by-event methods, on the other hand, process each event incrementally when it occurs, without any waiting time, with the aim of leveraging the low latency of the camera. Many event-by-event methods are inspired by the brain (i.e., neuromorphic), for example Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), since the neural circuits of visual processing are thought to be event-driven. Previous work proposes SNN architectures, but these comprise low-level physiological parameters of neurons (e.g., membrane potentials) that are difficult to interpret, validate and adjust in order to improve the estimation accuracy. In fact, insects and mammals have different low-level mechanisms, but they have similar algorithmic steps for transforming light into motion. So it is important to find the abstracted logical operations of motion estimation instead of mimicking all the physiological properties of neurons. Also, from a practical point of view, most event-by-event methods have only been tested on simple scenes, while batch-based methods are tested on more complex real-world scenes and publicly-available benchmarks. This may be because of the use of tailored hardware, strong assumptions about the scene, limited problem settings, or because it is difficult to define event-by-event benchmarks on real data with \mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s} resolution. So it is important to explore event-by-event motion estimation algorithms that can solve complex, real-world problems.

In this work we leverage insights from neuroscience, especially the classical Barlow-Levick model, and we propose a new optical flow estimation scheme that is based on correlation of occurrence. Unlike previous batch-based methods, it needs only three events (a triplet) for estimation, and this opens the door to real-time incremental motion estimation methods in the future. Unlike previous event-by-event approaches, we test it on publicly-available optical flow benchmarks to show that it can handle real-world scenes, with comparable results. It is also based on logical operations, so it can be implemented with a simple and efficient data structure and executed on standard CPUs. Our contributions are twofold: (i) we present a new event-by-event algorithm for optical flow estimation, which is derived theoretically from neuroscience insights, and (ii) we show in practice that it achieves comparable results to prior work while only needing a CPU and being faster than optimization-based algorithms (Fig. 1).

The signal processing in this work materializes the ideas in current neuroscience models, and it sheds light on the strong and weak scenarios, which can help to improve the models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Event cameras [1,2] have led to a rethinking of visual processing for various computer vision tasks because their operating principle and output data are fundamentally different from those of conventional, frame-based cameras. These bio-inspired sensors naturally respond to the scene dynamics and offer advantages, such as low latency, high dynamic range (HDR) and data efficiency, which need to be unlocked with new algorithms [3]. Neuromorphic principles have been a major source of inspiration for such novel algorithms and hardware, especially in motion estimation tasks [4,5,6].

Event-based optical flow estimation methods can be broadly classified as packet-based or event-by-event–based depending on how events are processed and update the estimator’s output. Packet-based methods process a batch of events (e.g., events in a fixed time window, say 10–100 ms, or a fixed number of events, typically 30k–1M), so they require some waiting time before processing (inference) starts [7,8,9,10]. They trade off the high-speed advantages of event data for accuracy. Prior work has proposed adaptations of classical frame-based methods (block matching [10], Lucas-Kanade [11]), spatio-temporal plane-fitting [8,12], time-surface matching [13], and contrast-maximization methods [14,7,9]. While the above methods are model-based (optimization) methods, Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) [15,16,17,18,19] are also batch-based, and are inspired by frame-based ANN architectures [20,21], thus requiring data conversion into a tensor representation, such as voxel grids. ANNs achieve current state-of-the-art accuracy for optical flow estimation and high speed [17,9], but require power-hungry GPUs and lack interpretability.

On the other hand, event-by-event methods process every event incrementally as it occurs (without waiting time), aiming to leverage the camera’s low-latency advantage [5,22]. Many event-by-event methods are inspired by the brain, such as Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) (i.e., neuromorphic), since the neural circuits of visual processing are thought to be event-driven. While previous work propose SNN architectures [23,24,6], they comprise low-level physiological parameters of neurons (e.g., membrane potentials) that are difficult to interpret, validate and adjust to improve the estimation accuracy. In fact, insects and mammals have different low-level underlying mechanisms, while they have similar algorithmic steps to transform light into motion [25]. Hence, it is important to find abstracted logical operations of motion estimation, rather than to mimic the entire physiological properties of neurons. From a practical point of view, most event-by-event methods have been tested on simple scenes, as opposed to the more complex real-world scenes and publicly-available benchmarks of batch-based methods [26]. This may be attributed to the use of tailored hardware [4], strong assumptions of the scene, limited problem settings [5] or the difficulty in defining event-by-event benchmarks on real data with \mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s} resolution. Hence, it is important to explore event-by-event motion estimation algorithms that can solve complex, real-world problems.

This work leverages insights from neuroscience, especially from the classical Barlow-Levick model [27], and proposes a novel optical flow estimation scheme based on correlation of occurrence. In contrast to previous batch-based methods, it requires only three events (triplet) for estimation, which could open the door to future real-time incremental motion estimation methods. Compared to previous event-by-event approaches, it is tested on publicly-available optical flow benchmarks to demonstrate its capability to handle real-world scenes with comparable results. It is also based on logical operations, which enables a simple and efficient data structure implementation and execution on standard CPUs. In summary, our contributions are twofold: (i) we present a novel event-by-event algorithm for optical flow estimation, theoretically derived from neuroscience insights, and (ii) we practically demonstrate that it achieves comparable results as prior work while only requiring a CPU and being faster than optimization-based algorithms (Fig. 1).

The signal processing in this work materializes the ideas in current neuroscience models, and sheds light on what the strong and weak scenarios are, so that the models can be improved.
